title: The Junk Shop of the Century: Balvanera, Corrientes, and the Words Argentina Uses About Itself
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Balvanera, and the Brother Who Raised Him

stops.name: Balvanera, the birth in a house of musicians
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Santos_Discépolo and the English article agree on 27 March 1901 at Balvanera.
stops.campa: In a house in Balvanera, a barrio of tenement courtyards and Neapolitan immigrants, Enrique Santos Discépolo is born on the twenty-seventh of March, youngest of five children in a family of musicians. He will die fifty years later a few streets from this room. Instruments stand about the house and the dialect of Naples is spoken alongside Spanish. Outside, Buenos Aires is absorbing a million arrivals, and the music those arrivals are making in the academias and the brothels of the port has no respectable name yet.
suggested_refs: The Balvanera parish registers and the conventillo blocks of the barrio at the turn of the century

stops.name: Balvanera, the brother takes the house
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sources record only that both parents died while Enrique was a child and that Armando, thirteen years his senior, took over his upbringing. No year is given anywhere consulted; 1906 orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: Both parents die while Enrique is still a child. The household passes to Armando, his brother, thirteen years older and already writing for the theater, who takes the boy in and takes him along to rehearsals and dressing rooms and the sainete companies working the city circuit. The younger brother's schooling happens backstage. What Armando is inventing in those years is the grotesco criollo, the immigrant comedy that turns without warning into a wound, the form Enrique will later compress into three minutes and a bandoneón. No source consulted gives the year the parents died.
suggested_refs: Armando Discépolo's grotesco criollo cycle, the theatrical form the younger brother grew up inside

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the stage beside Roberto Casaux
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only: es.wikipedia gives 1917 for the debut alongside Roberto Casaux; no month, and no playhouse is named. The coordinate is the canonical Buenos Aires pin used across this corpus, not a specific theater.
stops.campa: At sixteen he steps onto the stage himself, working beside Roberto Casaux, one of the best-known capocómicos in Buenos Aires. No source names the playhouse or the month. He is small, sharp-featured, restless, and the parts he gets are comic ones. For the next ten years the notices will keep telling him, in various tones, that he is not much of one. He keeps at it anyway, taking whatever the companies give him and writing at night. The theater district he works is six blocks of Corrientes. He wants to be an actor.
suggested_refs: The Roberto Casaux company and the Buenos Aires sainete circuit of the 1910s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first plays reach the stage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia lists El señor cura, El hombre solo and Día feriado under 1918. No premiere dates or houses are given.
stops.campa: A year after his debut three of his own plays reach the stage: El señor cura, El hombre solo, Día feriado. What the three of them set is a habit: that a piece is built out of a small number of people talking, that the talk is porteño street talk, and that it goes wrong. None of the plays survives in the repertory and no premiere date is recorded for any of them. He is seventeen, writing in the register his brother taught him, the one-act sainete with its conventillo courtyard and its cast of the barely solvent.
suggested_refs: El señor cura, El hombre solo, Día feriado (1918), his first staged texts

stops.name: Buenos Aires, acting in his brother's Mateo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia places his performance in Armando's Mateo in 1923 and their joint authorship of El organito in 1925.
stops.campa: He acts in Mateo, his brother's play about a coachman whose horse-drawn cab is being driven off the streets by the automobile, a man made obsolete inside a single decade and unable to say so. The lesson he takes from it he will spend twenty years restating in song: that the man ruined by the century does not know the word for what happened to him, and will therefore explain it as bad luck. Two years later the brothers write El organito together, Enrique inside Armando's theater now as performer and as collaborator both.
suggested_refs: Armando Discépolo, Mateo (1923) and El organito (1925), the second written with Enrique

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Bizcochito, the first music
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia dates Bizcochito to 1925. The research pool originally bundled it with Qué vachaché under 1925; that bundling is corrected here, Qué vachaché belonging to 1926.
stops.campa: He writes music for a tango called Bizcochito. It goes nowhere. What he has is a talent for the exact sentence in which somebody admits defeat, and the tango world he is entering has no use for it yet: the sung tango is eight years old, the record industry is pressing it by the crate, and the lyricists ahead of him write of neighborhoods and lost girls in a register of nostalgia. He has no gift for nostalgia. He is twenty-four and still principally a man of the theater, writing songs in the hours the theater leaves him.
suggested_refs: Bizcochito (1925), his first tango composition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Qué vachaché written
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qué_vachaché gives 1926 and credits both music and lyrics to Discépolo alone. The research pool's claim that he co-wrote it is corrected here.
stops.campa: He writes Qué vachaché, words and music both, and the thing that comes out is not a tango of loss but an argument: a woman telling a man that honesty is a luxury he cannot afford, that the century has priced decency out of the market and he had better learn to steal. It is 1926, eight years before Cambalache, and the whole later machine is already assembled here in miniature. Nobody wants it. The tango is offered around and finds no purchase in Buenos Aires.
stops.quote: El verdadero amor se ahogó en la sopa
stops.quote_source: Lyrics, Qué vachaché (1926), as quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qué_vachaché, where the article cites the line as prefiguring Cambalache
suggested_refs: Qué vachaché (1926), words and music by Discépolo

stops.name: Montevideo, the tango whistled off the stage
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place and failure, not as to date: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qué_vachaché records the Montevideo premiere by Mecha Delgado in 1926 with no month or venue. The Buenos Aires failure inside the revue Así da gusto vivir is separately dated 22 March 1926.
stops.campa: Across the river the tango gets its premiere, sung by Mecha Delgado in Montevideo, and the audience whistles it off the stage. The same year Tita Merello sings it in Buenos Aires at the Teatro Apolo, inside a revue called Así da gusto vivir, on the twenty-second of March, and that fails too. Two rejections in two cities in a single year, for a song whose argument is that the world rewards the thief. He goes back to the theater, where he is at least employed.
stops.quote: la panza es reina y el dinero es Dios
stops.quote_source: Lyrics, Qué vachaché (1926), as quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qué_vachaché
suggested_refs: Mecha Delgado's Montevideo premiere of Qué vachaché, 1926
The revue Así da gusto vivir, Teatro Apolo, Buenos Aires, 22 March 1926

stops.name: Folies Bergère, Tania at the cabaret
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) places the meeting at the Folies Bergère in 1927, with José Razzano making the introduction after hearing her sing Esta noche me emborracho. That song is dated 1928 everywhere consulted, so either the meeting is later or the song is earlier; the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: At the Folies Bergère cabaret he is introduced to a Spanish singer working Buenos Aires under the name Tania, born Ana Luciano Divis. Neither of them has yet had the success that will define them. From this evening they are together for the rest of his life: she sings what he writes, he stages what she performs, and she is in the room when he dies. The singer José Razzano makes the introduction, having heard her sing Esta noche me emborracho, a song every source dates a year after this evening.
suggested_refs: The Folies Bergère cabaret, Buenos Aires, and Tania's engagements there in the late 1920s

stops.name: Cangallo street, the apartment
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) names Cangallo street but gives no number, and no second source corroborates the address. The coordinate marks the street, not a building.
stops.campa: They move in together, into an apartment on Cangallo street a few blocks from the theaters. Tania has money from her own engagements and puts it into a production he is mounting; the arrangement between them is professional and domestic at once from the beginning, and it never becomes a marriage. She keeps the name Tania. He keeps the hours of a man who writes at night, and the rooms fill with the paper of unfinished lyrics, some of which he will carry unfinished for years.
suggested_refs: Calle Cangallo, Buenos Aires, renamed Teniente General Perón in 1984

segments.name: Esta Noche Me Emborracho: the Sudden Author

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Azucena Maizani carries the lyric
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Santos_Discépolo credits Azucena Maizani's performance of one of his compositions in 1928 with his first real notoriety, and Tita Merello's revival of another the same year. Neither article names which songs.
stops.campa: Azucena Maizani, one of the great voices of the decade, takes one of his tangos into her repertory, and the thing that failed twice in 1926 happens the other way round: the lyric travels the country on records, on the radio, in sheet music sold in the shops on Corrientes. Tita Merello revives another of his songs the same year and drives it to comparable reach. Inside twelve months he stops being a failed comic actor who writes on the side. Neither article names which songs the two women carried.
suggested_refs: Azucena Maizani's 1928 recordings; Tita Merello's revivals of Discépolo the same year

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Esta noche me emborracho and Chorra
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia lists both titles under 1928. The definition of tango quoted here is given at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango as his, with no further primary document behind it.
stops.campa: In one year he writes Esta noche me emborracho, in which a man meets on the street the woman he ruined himself over and finds her old, and Chorra, in which another man discovers that the woman he loved was working him for money the whole time and thanks her, bitterly, for the education. Both are in the first person and both are addressed to somebody. Both end with the speaker still talking, because stopping would mean thinking. His own definition of the form, repeated ever since without a document behind it, is that a tango is a sad thought that is danced.
stops.quote: un pensamiento triste que se baila
stops.quote_source: Definition of tango attributed to Discépolo, quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango; the article carries it without citing any primary document
suggested_refs: Esta noche me emborracho (1928); Chorra (1928)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Malevaje and Soy un arlequín
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the research pool dated Malevaje to 1929; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malevaje gives 1928, with music by Juan de Dios Filiberto and lyrics by Discépolo, who did not write the melody. Soy un arlequín stays at 1929. No month is attested for either; June orders the segment.
stops.campa: Juan de Dios Filiberto writes a melody and Discépolo writes words to it: Malevaje, the confession of a neighborhood tough who has fallen in love and can no longer fight, who cannot cross the street the way he used to, whose whole standing in the barrio has dissolved into a feeling he has no vocabulary for. The following year he writes Soy un arlequín. He is taking commissions now, working to other men's music, and the tangos arrive at a rate of several a year.
suggested_refs: Malevaje (1928), music Juan de Dios Filiberto, lyrics Discépolo
Soy un arlequín (1929)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the singers who carry his tangos
stops.date_confidence: the working relationship is attested [A]; the date is a marker, not an event. The remark about Ada Falcón is a two-layer attribution: his words survive only inside her own recollection, given in a 1995 interview, as recorded in ada_falcon.journey.json. It is not independently documented from the 1930s.
stops.campa: His tangos are now the property of the women who sing them. Azucena Maizani, Tita Merello, and Ada Falcón, whose recordings of his lyrics help pay for a three-storey house in Palermo Chico, work the same Odeón and Victor studios and the same radio hours, and he writes knowing which voice will take which line. What he said of Falcón survives only inside her own recollection, given in an interview in 1995, an old woman at the end of a long life quoting a young man forty-four years dead: so divine it does you harm to look at her.
stops.quote: so divine it does you harm to look at her
stops.quote_source: Discépolo on Ada Falcón, as she recalled it in a 1995 interview; recorded in ada_falcon.journey.json. English rendering; the Spanish original was not recovered in the sources consulted
suggested_refs: ada_falcon.journey.json, for Falcón's 1995 recollection of the remark
The Odeón and RCA Victor tango catalogues of the 1930s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Yira, yira
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yira,_yira dates the tango 1931, while the film of that name, in which he acts, is dated 1930 in his filmography. A film cannot easily precede the song it is named for; the sources are left in disagreement. The research pool's placement of the song in 1928 is supported by nothing consulted and is rejected.
stops.campa: He appears as an actor in a film called Yira, yira, and writes the tango of that name. The words are the plainest thing he ever wrote and the coldest: that you can go out looking for a hand to help you and find nothing, that indifference is the world's ordinary condition, that the wheel turns and does not care who is under it. It is the second year of a depression that has thrown men out of work across the country, and this time nobody whistles. The verb yirar is street Spanish for wandering, and for walking the streets to sell yourself.
suggested_refs: Yira, yira (1931), words and music by Discépolo
The film Yira, yira (1930), in which he acts

stops.name: Buenos Aires, directing Tania in Wunder Bar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) records that Discépolo directed her in Wunder Bar in Buenos Aires in 1933. No theater is named.
stops.campa: He directs Tania in Wunder Bar. The division of labor between them is settled by now: she performs, he stages her, and the theater remains what it has been since he was a boy following Armando to rehearsals, the trade he actually learned. The tangos get written between productions, at night, in the margins of a working life spent in rehearsal rooms. He is thirty-two and has not yet written the song that will outlive everything else he does. The sources name no theater and no month for the production.
suggested_refs: Wunder Bar, Buenos Aires production, 1933, directed by Discépolo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Cambalache written
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache gives 1934, both articles agreeing. No month for the writing.
stops.campa: He writes Cambalache. A cambalache is a junk shop, a place where a saint's image and a broken heater lie in the same window with no order between them, and he makes of it a description of the Argentina of the Década Infame: fraudulent elections, a country traded off, and a moral arithmetic in which the honest man and the thief have come to the same price. It is a list. It is almost the only tango he writes that is not addressed to a woman. It is addressed to the century.
stops.quote: Que el mundo fue y será una porquería, ya lo sé
stops.quote_source: Lyrics, Cambalache (1934), quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache as the song's most famous phrase
suggested_refs: Cambalache (1934), words and music by Discépolo

stops.name: Teatro Maipo, the premiere
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place and singer, approximate as to date: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache says the premiere came 'a fines de dicho año' with Sofía Bozán singing at Discépolo's own request. November orders the segment. The theater's coordinate is that of the Teatro Maipo at Esmeralda 449; the research pool placed the house on Avenida Corrientes, which is wrong.
stops.campa: At the Teatro Maipo on Esmeralda street, late in the year, the tango is sung for the first time by Sofía Bozán, La Negra, at Discépolo's own request. It is a revue house, and the song sits inside an evening of comic numbers. What the audience hears is a rhymed inventory delivered at speed, in which the twentieth century itself is the junk shop and everything sacred and everything filthy have been thrown into the same window. The state takes it off the radio in 1943.
stops.quote: Siglo veinte, cambalache, problemático y febril
suggested_refs: The Teatro Maipo, Esmeralda 449, San Nicolás
Sofía 'La Negra' Bozán, first interpreter of Cambalache

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Winter Garden with Tania
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) records his direction of her in Winter Garden in 1935. No venue or month.
stops.campa: He directs Tania again, in Winter Garden. Their theatrical partnership is in its ninth year and the work has begun to travel: the same season carries them out of Buenos Aires, across the river and over the cordillera. The revue form suits him. It is fast, it is cheap, it lets a song be dropped into an evening among comedians, and it is where Cambalache was first heard. He is the author of the most quoted lyric in the country and by his own arrangement of his days still a man of the theater, writing tangos between productions. He is thirty-four.
suggested_refs: Winter Garden, Buenos Aires production of 1935, directed by Discépolo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Cambalache goes into the cinema
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache records the song's use in the film El alma del bandoneón, sung by Ernesto Famá with Francisco Lomuto's orchestra, in 1935; the tango Alma del bandoneón is dated 1935 in his list of works. No month is given; June orders the segment.
stops.campa: The tango goes into the cinema: Ernesto Famá sings it with Francisco Lomuto's orchestra in the film El alma del bandoneón. Discépolo writes a tango of that title the same year, and it is his only composition dated to the whole of 1935. The song is now moving through every channel the country has: records, radio, film, the revue stage. The line about the Bible weeping against a water heater has begun to detach itself from the song and enter ordinary speech.
stops.quote: ves llorar la Biblia contra un calefón
stops.quote_source: Lyrics, Cambalache (1934), from the lyric block at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache. The popular phrase 'La Biblia y el calefón' derives from this line but is not itself a line of the song
suggested_refs: The film El alma del bandoneón (1935)
Alma del bandoneón (1935), tango

segments.name: The Tour, and the Turn to the Camera

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, over the cordillera
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) records a 1935 tour of Chile with Discépolo. No cities beyond the country, no months, no venues; the coordinate is Santiago as the country's principal stage and is a reasonable but unproven placement.
stops.campa: He and Tania cross the Andes and work Chile, part of a run of engagements that carries them out of the Río de la Plata entirely. Santiago knows his tangos from records before it sees him. The touring pattern of the Argentine tango world is well established by now, Montevideo and Santiago and Lima, and for those who can reach it Paris, and the singers move along it carrying a repertory written inside six blocks of Buenos Aires. Nothing survives of what he thought of the crossing.
suggested_refs: The 1935 Chilean engagements of Tania and Discépolo

stops.name: Montevideo, the other bank
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia records his theatrical success on the stages of Montevideo as well as Buenos Aires in this period, and Tania's article places Uruguay in the same 1935 run. No months, no houses named.
stops.campa: His theatrical work succeeds on the stages of Montevideo, the same city that whistled Qué vachaché off a stage nine years earlier. The two banks share one tango repertory and two accents; an author who has arrived in Buenos Aires has arrived here as well, and the crossing is a night boat. What it is to be applauded in the room where he was jeered he does not say anywhere. The Montevideo engagements belong to the same 1935 run as the Chilean ones.
suggested_refs: The Montevideo theatrical season of 1935

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the passage to Europe
stops.date_confidence: the journey is attested [A], the destination is not: es.wikipedia says only that he travelled to Europe in 1935 and turned to cinema on his return. No city, port, month, or itinerary is given anywhere consulted. The stop is pinned at Buenos Aires, the one place in the journey that is documented, rather than inventing a European coordinate. Tania's article places her own European tours in 1955-1959, after his death; there is no evidence she went with him.
stops.campa: He sails for Europe. His own biography records the journey and nothing else: no city, no dates, no account of what he saw or whom he played for, only that he went and that he came back with his intentions changed. What he brings home is a decision to work in film. Within two years he is inside the Argentine studios as actor, then as screenwriter, then as director, and the theater that raised him stops being where he spends his days. What happened over there to turn a playwright into a film director, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The 1935 European journey, undocumented beyond the fact of it

stops.name: Buenos Aires, into the studios
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: his filmography at es.wikipedia lists Mateo and Melodías porteñas as acting roles in 1937; Desencanto is dated 1936 in his list of works.
stops.campa: He acts in two films in one year: Mateo, the screen version of his brother's play about the ruined coachman, in which he had acted on stage fourteen years earlier, and Melodías porteñas. He has written Desencanto the year before. The Buenos Aires film industry is at its height, producing for the whole Spanish-speaking hemisphere, and it wants tango names. He is thirty-six, on a set instead of a stage, learning a trade for the second time. The theater work does not stop; it stops being the whole of the week.
suggested_refs: The films Mateo and Melodías porteñas (1937)
Desencanto (1936)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Cuatro corazones premieres
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuatro_corazones gives the premiere as 1 March 1939, co-directed with Carlos Schlieper, produced by Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos. The 1939 acting role in ...Y mañana serán hombres is from the same filmography.
stops.campa: Cuatro corazones opens on the first of March, co-directed with Carlos Schlieper: his first film as director, and he writes it and appears in it as well. He is thirty-seven. The same year he acts in ...Y mañana serán hombres. Nothing in the comedies he now makes resembles the tangos he is famous for. The man who wrote that the world was and always will be filth is spending the war years making people laugh for money. The films are light and quick and commercial, and they succeed.
suggested_refs: Cuatro corazones (1939), his first film as director

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the years as director
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years, from the filmography at es.wikipedia: Un señor mucamo and Caprichosa y millonaria and the screenplay of Confesión in 1940, En la luz de una estrella in 1941, Fantasmas en Buenos Aires in 1942, Cándida, la mujer del año in 1943. No months. 1941 is the midpoint and orders the segment.
stops.campa: Four years in the studios: Un señor mucamo and Caprichosa y millonaria and the screenplay of Confesión in 1940, En la luz de una estrella in 1941, Fantasmas en Buenos Aires in 1942, and Cándida, la mujer del año in 1943, the last film he directs. He is writing and directing at commercial pace, six pictures in four years, and the studios keep hiring him. Across the same stretch the tango output thins to almost nothing. Whatever he is carrying in these years, he is not putting it into songs, and no source consulted says why.
suggested_refs: The 1940-1943 directorial run, ending with Cándida, la mujer del año

segments.name: Uno: Three Years for a Lyric, and the Silence of the State

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mariano Mores hands him a melody
stops.date_confidence: attested [A] with a correction: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(tango) records that Mores gave Discépolo the score of a tango romanza called Cigarrillos en la oscuridad, that Discépolo wrote only the lyric, and that by Mores's own account it took him 'casi tres años'. The research pool's claim that Discépolo composed the music is wrong and is corrected here. 1943 is the year of completion; the handover is roughly three years earlier.
stops.campa: Mariano Mores, twenty-five years his junior, hands him the score of a tango romanza called Cigarrillos en la oscuridad and asks for a lyric. By Mores's own account Discépolo takes nearly three years over it. What he finally writes is the most exposed thing in his work: a man saying that he set out full of hope along the road his dreams had promised him, and arrived where he now is. They title it Si yo tuviera un corazón. The public asks for it by its first word, and the title becomes Uno.
stops.quote: Uno busca lleno de esperanzas el camino que los sueños prometieron a sus ansias
stops.quote_source: Lyrics, Uno (1943), music Mariano Mores, lyrics Enrique Santos Discépolo, quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(tango)
suggested_refs: Uno (1943), originally Si yo tuviera un corazón, on Mores's melody Cigarrillos en la oscuridad

stops.name: Teatro Astral, Uno sung by Tania
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(tango) gives April 1943, Teatro Astral, sung by Tania in the revue La revista loca. No day. The coordinate is the canonical Buenos Aires pin; the Teatro Astral's own coordinate was not established from the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Uno is premiered at the Teatro Astral in April, sung by Tania, inside a revue called La revista loca. She has been singing his work for sixteen years. The song is the confession of a man who has spent his heart and knows it, delivered by the woman who watched him spend it, in a variety house on Corrientes, between comic numbers. He is forty-two. It becomes almost at once the tango that other tangos are measured against, and no day of the month survives in the record.
suggested_refs: The revue La revista loca, Teatro Astral, April 1943

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the edict against lunfardo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, not the month: es.wikipedia records that from 1943 government censorship restricted tangos using lunfardo and references to drink and prostitution, and that Uno was kept off Buenos Aires radio. The Cambalache ban is separately dated from 1943 at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache. June is chosen to order the segment against the June 1943 coup and is not itself attested.
stops.campa: The military government issues directives against lunfardo on the radio, and against lyrics referring to drink, to prostitution, to the criminal barrio. Half the tango repertory is written in exactly that language. Cambalache is banned outright, Uno is kept off Buenos Aires radio, and singers are made to record laundered texts. The state has decided that the country's own popular music is not fit for the country to hear. Discépolo, whose whole subject is the language people actually use, loses his two best-known songs in the same year.
suggested_refs: The 1943 radio directives against lunfardo and their effect on the tango repertory

stops.name: Ambassador cinema, El fin de la noche withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(tango) records that the film, which carried Uno, was pulled from Buenos Aires cinemas by order of the Interior Ministry after one successful week, in November 1944. The Ambassador's own coordinate was not established; the canonical Buenos Aires pin stands in for it.
stops.campa: El fin de la noche, the film carrying Uno, plays one successful week at the Ambassador cinema and is then pulled from the screens by order of the Interior Ministry. The country is under a military government that has not declared against Germany and is watching what its cinemas say. A tango and a film are withdrawn together, by the same office. The ministry publishes no reason for either, and none has surfaced since. People go on singing the song.
suggested_refs: The Ambassador cinema, Buenos Aires, and the Interior Ministry withdrawal of November 1944

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the war declared and the film restored
stops.date_confidence: corrected and hedged: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(tango) says only that the film 'se la repondría recién en 1945' and gives no re-release date; its '25 de marzo' is an error, Argentina having declared war on Germany and Japan on 27 March 1945 by Decree 6945 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_during_World_War_II). The month of the re-release is unknown and defaults to January. Canción desesperada is dated 1944, not 1945, in his list of works.
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of March Argentina declares war on Germany and Japan, and the film is put back into the cinemas. No source gives the month of the re-release, or names the office that allowed it. The year before he had written Canción desesperada, a tango that asks who broke his wings and then answers itself. He is forty-four. Both the withdrawal and the restoration are decided in offices he has never entered. The ban on Cambalache holds four years more.
suggested_refs: Decree 6945 of 27 March 1945, Argentina's declaration of war
Canción desesperada (1944)

segments.name: Mexico, Havana, and the Son He Does Not Meet

stops.name: Mexico City, Raquel Díaz de León
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: both articles place a trip to Mexico in 1945 and a relationship there with the actress and journalist Raquel Díaz de León. No month, and the Spanish article names only 'México', not the capital; the coordinate is the canonical Mexico City pin used across this corpus.
stops.campa: He travels to Mexico. There he begins a relationship with Raquel Díaz de León, a Mexican actress and journalist. Tania is in his life and remains in it; the Mexican relationship runs alongside, is brief in the sources, and produces a child. Mexico City in these years is the other capital of Spanish-language cinema, full of Argentine and Spanish exiles and of studios that want tango names, and he is a known man there. What he does with his days in the city goes unrecorded.
suggested_refs: Raquel Díaz de León, Mexican actress and journalist

stops.name: Mexico City, the cabaret El Patio
stops.date_confidence: attested as to fact, not as to date [R]: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) records a gira with Discépolo through Cuba and Mexico, where she appeared at 'El Patio, el cabaret más relevante', and gives no year. The research pool's 1947 is unsupported; the surrounding text and his own biography point to the middle 1940s. The venue's own coordinate is unknown, so the city pin stands in.
stops.campa: He and Tania play El Patio, the leading cabaret of Mexico City. She sings; he is billed as the author of what she sings. The gira takes in Cuba as well, and the two of them are working the Caribbean and Mexican circuit that every major Argentine tango act works in these years, singing porteño lyrics about a specific six blocks of Corrientes to audiences who have never seen them. No date survives for the engagement, only that it happened, and that El Patio was the room that mattered.
suggested_refs: El Patio, Mexico City cabaret, and Tania's engagement there with Discépolo

stops.name: Havana, the tour goes on to Cuba
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: Cuba is named in Tania's article as part of the same gira with Discépolo, but no year, month, city, or venue is given. Havana is the reasonable placement for a Cuban engagement and is not itself attested; the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The tour goes on to Cuba. Tania sings, and the tangos she carries are the ones that have already made the crossing on record: Esta noche me emborracho, Yira, yira, Uno. Cuba has its own dance music and takes the tango as a foreign melancholy, elegant and a little comic, a thing played late and danced by couples who hold themselves very straight. Which city, which rooms, which year: none of it is in the sources consulted. The order survives and nothing else, Mexico first and then Cuba, the two of them travelling together.
suggested_refs: The Cuban leg of the Tania and Discépolo gira, undated in the sources

stops.name: Mexico, the son he does not meet
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the child's dates, contradictory as to the sequence: en.wikipedia and es.wikipedia give Enrique Luis Santos Discépolo Díaz de León, born 21 April 1947, died 28 May 2017, and say Discépolo never met him. The Spanish article dates the Mexican journey to 1945 and gives the place only as 'México', not the capital. A April 1947 birth implies conception around July 1946; the further claim that he left when she was six months pregnant was not found in the article text retrieved and cannot be squared with a stay confined to 1945. The gap is left open.
stops.campa: A son is born to Raquel Díaz de León on the twenty-first of April and given his father's name: Enrique Luis Santos Discépolo Díaz de León. Discépolo never meets him. The boy will live seventy years and die in 2017. The sources put the Mexican journey in 1945 and the birth in 1947 and do not explain the two years between them; they also say he left when she was six months pregnant, which those two dates cannot both accommodate. The child is the only one he has.
suggested_refs: Enrique Luis Santos Discépolo Díaz de León (1947-2017)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a new lyric for El Choclo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, from angel_villoldo.journey.json and the sources behind it: Discépolo's wholly new 1947 lyric for Villoldo's El Choclo, and Libertad Lamarque's premiere of it in Luis Buñuel's Gran Casino. No month is given.
stops.campa: Ángel Villoldo has been dead twenty-eight years. His El Choclo, written before the century turned, is the oldest tango anyone still plays, and Discépolo writes it a wholly new lyric, beginning with the tango itself speaking, mocking and swaggering. The words take. Within a few years the Villoldo text is the one nobody sings and the Discépolo text is what El Choclo means, the melody carrying on underneath unaltered, belonging to a man who never heard either version sung this way. Libertad Lamarque premieres the new words in Gran Casino, Luis Buñuel's first Mexican film.
stops.quote: Con este tango que es burlón y compadrito
stops.quote_source: Opening line of Discépolo's 1947 lyric for El Choclo, as recorded in angel_villoldo.journey.json
suggested_refs: angel_villoldo.journey.json, for the tango's origin and its later lyric history
Gran Casino (1947), directed by Luis Buñuel, with Libertad Lamarque and Jorge Negrete

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Cafetín de Buenos Aires in a week
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafetín_de_Buenos_Aires records that Mores gave him a melody written for a film scene and asked for lyrics within a week, and that he delivered on the deadline. No month for the commission.
stops.campa: Mariano Mores hands him another melody, written for a scene in a film, and asks for the lyric inside a week. Discépolo, who took three years over Uno, delivers on the deadline. What he delivers in seven days is Cafetín de Buenos Aires, in which a grown man addresses the café of his adolescence as the place that taught him everything he knows, philosophy and dice and the cruel poetry of thinking about nothing. It is the least bitter thing he ever wrote, and the most grateful.
stops.quote: Me diste en oro un puñado de amigos
stops.quote_source: Lyrics, Cafetín de Buenos Aires (1948), quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafetín_de_Buenos_Aires
suggested_refs: Cafetín de Buenos Aires (1948), music Mariano Mores, lyrics Discépolo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Tania and Rivero record the Cafetín
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafetín_de_Buenos_Aires gives 1 July 1948 for Tania's recording with Héctor Stamponi's orchestra and places Edmundo Rivero's, with Aníbal Troilo's orchestra, a week later.
stops.campa: On the first of July Tania records the tango with Héctor Stamponi's orchestra. A week later Edmundo Rivero records it with Aníbal Troilo's, and it is Rivero's version, that enormous low voice over Troilo's bandoneón, that fixes it. Phrases come out of the song and into the street within months, used daily by people who could not name the author: the know-alls and the suicides at the back tables, the child with his nose flattened against the café window.
stops.quote_source: A phrase from Cafetín de Buenos Aires that entered popular speech, so described at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafetín_de_Buenos_Aires, together with 'los sabihondos y suicidas'. The article presents both as phrases extracted from the letra, not as verbatim lines
suggested_refs: Edmundo Rivero's 1948 recording with the Aníbal Troilo orchestra
Tania's 1948 recording with Héctor Stamponi

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Perón lifts the ban
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the meeting and the order, per es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambalache. Note a discrepancy inside the research pool: the same 25 March 1949 event is described in one lens as lifting the ban on Cambalache and in another as lifting the ban on Uno. The Cambalache article is the source that carries the date, so Cambalache is followed here and the other reading is flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Directors of SADAIC obtain a meeting with President Perón and put it to him that Cambalache has been off the radio for six years. Perón says he did not know the directives existed and orders them lifted. The most quoted lyric in Argentina goes back on the air by presidential word, and Discépolo, who has spent the decade being censored by successive governments, is now in debt to this one. He is a Peronist already, out of conviction and before the favor. The meeting does not make him one.
suggested_refs: The SADAIC delegation to Perón, 25 March 1949

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Corrientes, calle de ensueños
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafetín_de_Buenos_Aires dates the film's release to September 1949. Yo no elegí mi vida, which he wrote and acted in, is dated 1949 in his filmography without a month.
stops.campa: Corrientes, calle de ensueños reaches the cinemas in September, carrying Cafetín de Buenos Aires. The song is a year old and its phrases are already in the street. The same year he writes and acts in Yo no elegí mi vida, whose title is a sentence any one of his characters could have said. He is forty-eight and has written four or five songs the country will never stop singing. There is one more film ahead of him, which he will write and appear in. After that the work is radio, and the work is arguing.
suggested_refs: Corrientes, calle de ensueños (1949)
Yo no elegí mi vida (1949)

segments.name: Mordisquito, and the Room in Balvanera

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mordisquito on the radio
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the research pool dated the Mordisquito broadcasts to 1947, four years too early. es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordisquito,_a_mí_no_me_la_vas_a_contar records that Raúl Apold convened him to write monologues defending state policy ahead of the November 1951 presidential election, and the biography places the Peronist conflict, per Pichon-Rivière, between 1950 and 1951. No month is attested; January orders the segment.
stops.campa: Raúl Apold, the government's press secretary, calls him in to write a series of radio monologues defending the state's policies before the November presidential election. Discépolo invents an antagonist to argue with, a man he names Mordisquito, who is every complaint he has ever heard against Peronism, and he takes him apart nightly on the air, calling the opposition sheep of the oligarchy and cipayos. The scripts pass through Apold's office for approval before they are read.
stops.quote_source: Discépolo's terms for his opponents in the Mordisquito broadcasts, as quoted at es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Santos_Discépolo, alongside 'cipayos'
suggested_refs: Mordisquito, a mí no me la vas a contar, the 1951 radio monologues
Raúl Apold's Subsecretaría de Informaciones and its approval of the scripts

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the houses bought empty
stops.date_confidence: attested as to fact, undated as to occasion: es.wikipedia records that opponents bought out entire theater houses so that his performances played to empty seats, and that this came from people he considered friends. It also carries Pichon-Rivière's account of a strong conflict of ambivalence in his final years, placed 1950-1951. March 1951 orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: The answer comes from the other side. Anti-Peronists buy out entire theaters where he is appearing, so that he walks onto the stage and plays to rows of paid-for empty seats, night after night. The people doing it include men he had counted as friends. His circle records that it fills him with a profound sadness. Enrique Pichon-Rivière, the psychoanalyst, his friend, sets down that in these last years Discépolo suffered a strong conflict of ambivalence about the government he was defending.
suggested_refs: Enrique Pichon-Rivière's account of Discépolo's final years

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El hincha, the last film
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: es.wikipedia gives 13 April 1951 for El hincha, which he wrote and in which he took his final screen role.
stops.campa: El hincha opens on the thirteenth of April. He wrote it and he acts in it, playing a football supporter, a man whose whole life is given over to a club that does not know his name. It is the last time he appears on a screen. The character is one more of his obsessives, a man devoted past all proportion to something that cannot return the devotion, and the register is affectionate rather than savage, which is where he has ended up. He is fifty and has eight months to live.
suggested_refs: El hincha (1951), written by Discépolo, his last screen role

stops.name: Balvanera, the death
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Santos_Discépolo and es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_(cantante) both give 23 December 1951. The English article contradicts itself internally, its infobox giving 27 December and its body text 24 December. Three dates are therefore in circulation. The Spanish articles are followed here because two of them agree independently; the contradiction is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: He dies in Balvanera, the barrio he was born in, of a heart attack, cancer compounding it, with Tania at his side. He is fifty years old. His friends do not separate the illness from the year he has just had, the bought-out houses and the conflict Pichon-Rivière recorded, and his biographers link the two as well. The date his own country keeps is the twenty-third of December. Two other days are in circulation, in a single foreign article that carries both of them at once.
suggested_refs: The death notices of December 1951 and the disagreement among them

stops.name: La Chacarita, the pantheon of SADAIC
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month only: es.wikipedia records burial in the Panteón de la Sociedad Argentina de Autores y Compositores, a private pantheon for musicians and composers inside the Cementerio de la Chacarita, in December 1951; no day is given, and 24 December follows the death by one day as an ordering device. The coordinate is the cemetery's own, per es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cementerio_de_la_Chacarita; the two coordinates supplied in the research pool for this grave disagreed with each other and both were off the cemetery.
stops.campa: He is buried in La Chacarita, in the pantheon the Sociedad Argentina de Autores y Compositores keeps for its own inside the cemetery, among the musicians, a few streets north of the barrio where he was born and where he died. Tania inherits his composer's rights to forty-two works and spends the rest of her life tending them; she is laid in the same ground long afterward. On Avenida Corrientes at the nine hundred block, where a street now carries his name, plaques mark the corner as the esquina de Discépolo.
suggested_refs: The Panteón de SADAIC, Cementerio de la Chacarita
The plaques at Avenida Corrientes al 900 and calle Enrique Santos Discépolo
